title: The flexible fifth moves
intro:
Black neither props up e5 with a pawn nor pins the knight, but develops and waits. Four moves come up often enough to know: 5...Qd6, 5...Bd6, 5...Qf6 and 5...Ne7.

## What they have in common

All four leave the pawn on e5 defended by a piece rather than a pawn, so d4 is nearly always the answer. Once White plays it Black has to take, and the moment the e-pawns come off the majority is fixed and the rest of the game is the one this course is about.

## Where each one goes

5...Qd6 is the most solid. The queen holds e5 and gets out of the rooks' way, and the answer is 6.Na3, which looks wrong and is heading for c4 with a hit on her.

5...Bd6 and 5...Qf6 both hold e5 with a piece that can be hit, so d4 comes with tempo. After 5...Bd6 6.d4 exd4 7.Qxd4, watch what happens to g7: 7...Ne7 loses a pawn to 8.Qxg7, and it is exactly the move a club player makes without a thought.

5...Ne7 is the one with a capture in it. The knight walks away from the defence of e5 and leaves it to a pawn that is still at home, so 6.Nxe5 is on. Black's main try is 6...Qd4, hitting the knight and e4 at once, and 7.Qh5 defends the knight and threatens f7 in the same move.

## The habit this chapter is really teaching

Count what is defending e5 before every capture. In four of this course's six chapters something is, and taking loses a piece. Here it is not, and taking wins a pawn. The difference is one look.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Playing d4 without counting first. Taking a queen trade that did not have to be taken. Recapturing on d4 with the knight and losing it to the pawn on c5. And missing 8.Qxg7 when the knight leaves g7 undefended.
